title: Optimal control for duty-cycle-limited interferometry with single-NV centers
authors: Ugur Tamer, Sina Zeytinoglu, Ozgur E. Mustecaplioglu
abstract: Stimulus-responsive hydrogels convert temperature changes into magnetic-field shifts detectable by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, enabling nanoscale thermometry in soft and biological environments. Existing hydrogel-nanodiamond demonstrations rely on NV ensembles, whose high photon throughput is accompanied by gradient-induced inhomogeneous broadening, while idealized single-NV projections assume high-fluence fluorescence/ODMR readout. Here we study a pulsed single-NV route for the same class of sensors and ask whether decoherence-aware coherent control can improve thermometric performance over optimized Ramsey interrogation at equal detected-photon budget. Using a sigmoidal volume-phase-transition model, dipolar magnetic transduction, and Lindblad master-equation simulations, we find a reproducible 25-27% per-shot sensitivity gain over optimized Ramsey, i.e., a 57-60% gain in Fisher information (1.57-1.60). The same gain carries over to the photon-normalized Fisher information. The rate gain is governed by the measurement duty cycle, the fraction of the experimental cycle spent accumulating signal rather than initializing, reading out or waiting, and becomes largest when the overhead or optical-dose constraint dominates the cycle time. The optimized trajectories reveal a response-shaping mechanism in which phase accumulation is concentrated near the end of the sequence, and a closed-form depth-two solution reproduces the numerical optimum and exhibits that mechanism analytically. The advantage is most pronounced when the dephasing time is short compared with the measurement overhead or dose-limited waiting time, which is the operating regime targeted by hydrogel-transduced single-spin biosensing.
summary: This paper develops an optimal control strategy for enhancing temperature sensing using single NV centers coupled to hydrogels. By implementing QSP-inspired coherent control sequences, the authors demonstrate a significant gain in measurement sensitivity (up to 60% in Fisher information) compared to standard Ramsey methods. This shows that optimizing the measurement sequence, rather than just the physical setup, is crucial for high-performance quantum sensing in practical settings.
main_problem: The paper aims to improve the sensitivity of temperature measurements using single Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in hydrogels, particularly when the measurement is limited by the duty cycle.
main_result: The authors achieved a reproducible 25–27% per-shot sensitivity gain over optimized Ramsey interrogation, corresponding to a 57–60% gain in Fisher information.
method: They employed quantum control techniques, specifically QSP-inspired coherent control, applied to a pulsed single-NV measurement sequence.
model_or_system: The system involves single NV centers coupled to stimulus-responsive hydrogels, which transduce temperature changes into magnetic field shifts. The physics is modeled using a sigmoidal volume-phase-transition model and simulated via Lindblad master equations.
key_observables: Per-shot sensitivity gain, Fisher information gain, and the rate gain governed by the measurement duty cycle.
important_parameters: The advantage is most pronounced when the dephasing time ($T_2$) is short compared with the measurement overhead or dose-limited waiting time.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a point-dipole magnetic field and that the primary decoherence mechanism is dephasing ($\sigma_z$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the sensor (hydrogel states), the comparison of signal envelopes (calibrated vs. uncalibrated), and global gain maps showing the dependence on control depth and time.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by modeling the temperature-to-field transduction, comparing standard Ramsey interrogation against optimized coherent control protocols, and deriving the resulting sensitivity gains.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the optimization of quantum sensing protocols in realistic, resource-constrained environments (like biosensing), providing quantitative gains by optimizing the measurement sequence itself.

This photon-budget result belongs to the pulsed single- NV model. The control gain is obtained at the same detected-photon budget per shot as optimized Ramsey.
